newsitem.title: USA: FDA decision soon on beef irradiation - official.
newsitem.headline: FDA decision soon on beef irradiation - official.

text.p: The Food and Drug Administration will be making a long awaited decision "in the not too distant future" on whether to approve irradiation of beef as a way to kill foodborne bacteria, a senior FDA official said Wednesday.

In response to a question at a seminar on food safety, Fred Shank, director of FDA's Centre for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition, said, "The (irradiation) petition on red meat is currently being evaluated, and you can expect a decision in the not too distant future."
An FDA spokesman said Shank's comments indicated a decision could be out within the next several months.

Thomas Billy, administrator of the Agriculture Department's Food Safety and Inspection Service, commented after Shank that USDA thinks irradiation is an important technology, and said, "We see its application in the future."
Billy and Shank were participants in a panel discussion on the administration's new food safety initiative.
An irradiation facility filed a petition with FDA in July 1994 to irradiate beef products. The meat industry has supported that petition.

The FDA has already approved irradiating pork and poultry to prevent bacteria. An FDA spokesman said the complexity of the issue, along with a fairly small scientific staff, has accounted for the long review period.
"We would be delighted if they responded favorably to the petition," said Sarah Clark Lilygren of the American Meat Institute. " We don't understand why it's taken so long."

Irradiation has been touted by its supporters as an effective and safe way to kill off dangerous foodborne bacteria, but questioned by others who allege that it changes the texture and taste of the food product.
Lilygren compared the process to "an extreme form of microwave that destroys bacteria without cooking the product."

Industry officials did not predict meat irradiation to immediately become widespread if the process is approved, citing costs and logistics as limiting factors, but said it would provide meat processors with another valuable tool to kill bacteria in their products.
